lessons.title: How Markets Actually Work
lessons.content:
# Day 1 — How Markets Actually Work

**🎬 The story of 45 minutes that broke Wall Street's brain**

On May 6, 2010, at 2:32 PM New York time, the Dow Jones was having a bad but ordinary
day — down about 300 points. Then, in the next 36 minutes, it fell nearly 1,000 points
more. For a few minutes, shares of the consulting firm Accenture traded at **one cent**.
PG&E — a boring, stable utility — traded at **$39,999.99** a share. P&G itself crashed
37% in minutes, then recovered almost everything before the closing bell.

No asteroid hit. No bank collapsed. What happened was simpler and more important:
one large mutual-fund company started selling about **$4.1 billion** worth of
stock-market bets, all at once, into a market where buyers had quietly stepped away. For a few minutes, there were almost no agreements between buyers and
sellers at *any* price. So prices — remember, prices are just the last agreement —
printed absurd numbers until buyers returned. The SEC later called it the Flash Crash.

Sit with that: the most sophisticated market on Earth briefly priced Accenture at 1
cent and a power company at $39,999.99. Not because anyone decided those were fair
prices — but because those were the last agreements between the few buyers and sellers
still standing.

**That is the entire subject of today's lesson.** Once you truly understand what a price
is, 80% of trading confusion evaporates.

> 💬 **Before we start — honest answers only:** if you'd had money in the market on March 13, 2020 (the day Nifty froze at the lower circuit), do you think you'd have been one of the people frantically pressing *sell*… or one of the frozen watchers refreshing the app? There's no wrong answer. Yet. Jot down your guess — by tonight you'll know exactly what you'd have been watching.

## What you'll learn
- What a "price" actually is (the Flash Crash makes it obvious)
- Why prices move up and down
- Who you're trading against

## A market is an auction — nothing more

Forget the news, the indicators, the opinions. At its core, every market is an auction
with one item for sale and millions of bidders.

- A **buyer** says: *"I'll pay ₹24,100 for one Nifty futures contract."*
- A **seller** says: *"I'll only sell at ₹24,120."*
- When a buyer agrees to pay the seller's price (or vice versa), a **trade happens** —
  and the price on your screen updates to that last traded price.

**The price on your screen is simply the price of the most recent agreement between one
buyer and one seller.** Accenture at ₹0.01 wasn't a valuation — it was the last
agreement in a temporarily empty room.

## Why prices move

Prices move for one reason only:

> **When aggressive buyers outnumber aggressive sellers, price rises. When aggressive
> sellers outnumber aggressive buyers, price falls.**

- **Aggressive buyer** = someone who hits "buy now" and accepts the seller's asking price.
- **Aggressive seller** = someone who hits "sell now" and accepts the buyer's price.

If 1,000 people suddenly want to buy and only 200 want to sell at the current price,
the buyers consume the available sellers. The next sellers demand more. Price rises.
The Flash Crash was the extreme version: sellers screamed, buyers vanished, and price
fell off a cliff until new buyers found the prices attractive enough to agree again.

## Who is on the other side of your trade?

You are never trading against "the market." You're trading against *people*:

| Participant | What they want | How it shows up |
|---|---|---|
| Retail traders (like you) | Quick profits | Small, scattered orders |
| Institutions (mutual funds, FIIs/DIIs) | Fill huge positions over days | Sustained one-directional moves |
| Market makers | Earn the spread, stay flat | Constant two-sided quotes |
| Hedgers | Protect existing holdings | Predictable orders at levels |

Beginners imagine they're trading against geniuses. Mostly you're trading against
*patterns of behavior* — and behavior repeats. That's why price patterns exist at all.

## 📌 Case file: March 2020 — the panic you will live through again

Between February 19 and March 23, 2020, the S&P 500 fell **34% in 23 trading days** —
the fastest bear market in history. Nifty did the same in lockstep. News readers were
paralyzed; auction readers saw something simpler: aggressive sellers everywhere, buyers
only at lower and lower prices. Every day, the last agreement printed lower. Then on
March 23, buyers stepped back in aggressively — and the same mechanism ran in reverse:
the S&P rose roughly 50% in five months and made new all-time highs by August.

No prediction was needed. Only the ability to read *who is more aggressive right now* —
the skill this course builds from the ground up.

## 🇮🇳 The Indian story: circuits, panic, and the 7,511 bottom

You lived the Indian version of the Flash Crash. On March 13, 2020, Nifty hit its 10%
lower circuit within minutes of opening — trading was frozen, and thousands of sell
orders sat frozen with it. On March 23, it happened again, and Nifty touched **7,511
intraday** — down ~39% in five weeks. India VIX, the fear gauge, spiked past **83**, the
highest reading anywhere in the world at that time. Same mechanism as May 2010: sellers
screaming, buyers gone, last agreements printing lower by the minute. Then, on March 24,
buyers stepped back in aggressively — and Nifty roughly **doubled within eight months**,
closing 2020 near 13,982. No prediction needed — just reading who was more aggressive,
day by day.

## Key takeaways
- Price = the most recent agreement between a buyer and a seller. (Flash Crash: 1 cent
  to $39,999.99 proves it.)
- Price moves when one side becomes more aggressive than the other.
- You trade against repeating human behavior, not against "the market."

## Quick check ✅
1. Price on your screen updates when…?
2. If buyers keep "eating" all available sellers at the ask, what happens next?
3. True or false: a big green candle means more people bought than sold at that moment.

## Today's action step
Open your charting app, put Nifty 50 on a 5-minute chart, and watch it live for 10 minutes
(no trading). Don't look for patterns — narrate the auction like a commentator: *"Sellers
pushing, buyers waiting… buyers stepped in, sellers pulled their orders…"* You're
training the exact muscle that read March 2020 in real time.

📊 CHART NEEDED: `charts/L1-01-nifty-auction.png`
INSTRUMENT / TIMEFRAME: Nifty 50 · 5-minute
MUST SHOW:
  - One large bullish candle (e.g., a 30–40 point 5-min candle)
  - An annotation arrow: "Aggressive buyers stepped in here"
  - A small zone marked below the candle: "Sellers absorbed — no one left to sell"

Answers: 1 — a trade executes at a new price · 2 — price rises as sellers demand more ·
3 — True (aggressive buyers outnumbered sellers)

# Day 2 — Brokers & Order Types

**🎬 The 45 minutes that cost $440 million**

On August 1, 2012, Knight Capital — one of the largest market makers in America,
handling trades for everyday investors — deployed a software update. One line of dead
code from an old module woke up. Within **45 minutes**, Knight's machines had sent
millions of unintended orders into the stock market, buying high and selling low in a
loop it couldn't stop. By the time engineers killed it: **$440 million gone — roughly
$170,000 per second**. Knight's stock collapsed 60%+ and the firm was rescued in a
fire-sale merger days later.

Here's why this story opens a lesson for *you*: Knight's disaster wasn't about analysis.
It was about **the plumbing** — what happens between your finger pressing "buy" and the
exchange matching your order. That plumbing is the broker's world, and you live in it
every trade. Today you learn the four order types that control exactly how your bid
enters that auction.

> 💬 **Quick honesty check:** when you open your trading app, do you actually know *where your shares are held*? If your broker's app vanished tomorrow, could you get your holdings back? Jot your guess in your head — today's two stories will make you want to check. What do you think — safe, or "never thought about it"?

## What you'll learn
- What a broker actually does (and Knight's place in the chain)
- Market, limit, stop-market and stop-limit orders
- Which order type to use when

## What a broker does

You can't walk up to the exchange and shout your order. A **broker** is your licensed
gateway: your app sends an order → the broker validates and routes it → the exchange
matches it against another order → the fill comes back to you — all in milliseconds.

In the chain, your broker also: holds your money, calculates margin, sends contract
notes, and reports your trades to tax authorities. (And a broker's own systems can fail —
Knight's did; so can your app's. **Choose a broker you trust with money and data.** On
volatile days in India, you've probably seen screenshots of broker outages; the traders
who planned for it had phone-trade backups. The plumbing matters.)

## The four order types

### 1. Market order — "Get me in NOW"
You accept whatever price is available right now.
- ✅ Guaranteed fill, instantly
- ❌ No price guarantee — in a fast market you get a worse price (*slippage*, Day 6).
  Knight's rogue orders were effectively toxic market orders.
- **Use when:** exiting a losing trade fast. *Never* for careful entries.

### 2. Limit order — "Only at my price (or better)"
You name your price. The order sits in the queue until someone accepts it.
- ✅ Guaranteed price (or better)
- ❌ Not guaranteed to fill — price may run away without you
- **Use when:** planning an entry at a level you chose in advance. **Your default order
  type for entries.**

### 3. Stop-market order — "If price hits X, get me out NOW"
Dormant until price touches your *trigger*, then becomes a market order.
- ✅ Your safety net — this is what a stop loss is
- ❌ In a panic, fills can be far from the trigger price
- **Use when:** always, on every trade, no exceptions.

### 4. Stop-limit order — "If price hits X, place a limit at Y"
Dormant until trigger, then becomes a *limit* order.
- ✅ Price control after the trigger
- ❌ Dangerous: in a crash your limit may never fill and you ride the whole fall
- **Use when:** rarely, only once experienced. Beginners skip this.

📊 CHART NEEDED: `charts/L1-02-order-types.png`
INSTRUMENT / TIMEFRAME: Any liquid stock · 15-minute
MUST SHOW:
  - Current price marked clearly
  - Dashed line above price: "Stop-market trigger (buy stop / stop loss for shorts)"
  - Dashed line below price: "Limit buy entry"
  - Dashed line lower: "Stop loss trigger (sell stop)"

## 📌 Case file: January 2021 — the buy button disappeared

During the GameStop mania, on January 28, 2021, Robinhood — the broker of millions of
new traders — suddenly *removed the buy button* on GameStop and a handful of other
stocks. Traders could sell, not buy. Furious users sued; Congress held hearings. Robinhood
said margin requirements from its clearinghouse had exploded overnight — the plumbing
again: when volatility explodes, the system demands more collateral, and brokers can
choke. Whatever you think of the politics, the lesson for a trader is permanent:
**know your broker's rules, know the order types cold, and never assume the button will
be there when you most need it.**

## 🇮🇳 The Indian story: Karvy and the broker you trusted

India got its own plumbing scandal. Karvy Stock Broking — a **90-year-old, respected
hyderabad brokerage** — was barred by SEBI in late 2019 for pledging client securities
worth roughly **₹2,300 crore** to raise loans for itself. Clients who thought their
shares sat safely in their accounts discovered they'd been mortgaged. The lesson is
Knight Capital's lesson at Indian scale: the chain between you and the exchange —
broker, depository, margins, order routing — is invisible until the day it matters.
Know your broker's financial health, keep your holdings visible in your own demat
statements, and always know which of your order types protects you when the app hangs
on a circuit day.

## Key takeaways
- Market = speed, limit = price, stop-market = protection, stop-limit = advanced.
- Your default entry: limit order at a level you chose. Your default protection:
  stop-market on every single trade.
- The Knight/Robinhood stories: the plumbing IS the product. Respect it.

## Quick check ✅
1. You want to buy Reliance only if it drops to ₹2,900. Which order?
2. You own a stock at ₹500 and want to auto-exit if it falls to ₹480. Which order?
3. Why is stop-limit risky as a stop loss in a crash?

## Today's action step
Open your broker's order window (don't place anything) and identify every field:
instrument, quantity, order type, price, trigger price, validity (DAY/IOC). Touch each
one so the screen feels familiar before real money is involved. Then find your broker's
policy page on margin and outages — two minutes of boredom that might save your account
one day.

Answers: 1 — Limit buy at ₹2,900 · 2 — Stop-market, trigger ₹480 ·
3 — The limit may never fill in a fast fall, leaving you exposed

# Day 3 — Reading Charts: Candles, Timeframes & Volume

**🎬 One tweet, one candle, $365 billion gone**

On May 13, 2021, at 6:06 PM, Elon Musk tweeted that Tesla would stop accepting Bitcoin
for environmental reasons. Within hours, Bitcoin printed a candle that fell from roughly
$54,000 to below $46,000 — nearly **$365 billion wiped off crypto's total value in a
single move**. Six days later, on May 19, a second wave hit: China reiterated its crypto
ban, and Bitcoin dropped 30% in a day, at one point 50% below its April high.

If you'd looked at those days on a chart, you wouldn't have needed the news first — the
candles *told* you. A giant red body with a long lower wick: sellers slammed price down,
buyers fought back at the lows. Volume bars three times the normal height: this wasn't
retail noise, it was a stampede. Today you learn to read exactly that language.

> 💬 **Try this before reading on:** open any chart you have and look at the last candle for five full seconds. Don't scroll, don't analyze. Just look. What do you think it's saying? Hold that guess — by the end of today, you'll read that candle the way you read a headline. Write your first impression in your notes if you like.

## What you'll learn
- Anatomy of a candlestick (using the May 2021 dump)
- How to read any timeframe
- What volume tells you that price hides

## Anatomy of a candlestick

A candle compresses four prices from its time period into one picture: **Open** (start),
**Close** (end), **High** and **Low** (the extremes). The thick **body** spans open →
close; the thin **wicks** show the high/low excursions.

- **Bullish candle** (green): close *above* open → buyers won the period
- **Bearish candle** (red): close *below* open → sellers won the period

✅ Diagram already made: `charts/generated/L1-03-candle-anatomy.png`

**Read the wicks like a fight replay:** on May 19, 2021, Bitcoin's daily candle had a
massive *lower* wick — sellers pushed it down ~50% from the April top, and buyers
rejected those prices so hard that the candle closed far off its low. That long lower
wick was the first footprint of the bottoming process. A long *upper* wick is the
mirror: buyers pushed up and got slapped back. Wicks are footprints of who lost the fight.

## Timeframes: the same movie, different zoom

A timeframe is just how long each candle represents:

| Timeframe | Each candle = | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| 1D (daily) | One full day | "What's the big picture trend?" |
| 1H | One hour | "Where are institutions active?" |
| 15m / 5m | 15 / 5 minutes | "Where exactly do I enter?" |
| 1m | One minute | Scalping territory — ignore for now |

> **Golden rule:** the lower the timeframe, the more noise. During the May 2021 crash,
the *daily* candle told a clear story of panic-then-defense. The *1-minute* chart that
day was a seizure — thousands of whipsaws that would have triggered and stopped out
anything mechanical. Same event, different truth, depending on zoom.

📊 CHART NEEDED: `charts/L1-03-nifty-timeframes.png`
INSTRUMENT / TIMEFRAME: Nifty 50 · same date range on 1D, 1H, 15m, 5m (4 panels)
MUST SHOW:
  - The exact same swing visible on all four panels
  - Labels: 1D "Trend" / 1H "Structure" / 15m "Setup" / 5m "Entry trigger"

## Volume: the lie detector

**Volume** = how many contracts/shares changed hands in that candle. Price tells you
*where*; volume tells you *how much conviction* was behind it.

- Big move + big volume → real move (May 19, 2021: record volume, real repricing)
- Big move + tiny volume → suspect move, often reverses
- Breakout + volume spike → the breakout is genuine

During March 2020, global exchanges printed their highest volumes in history — the
crash was real, and so was the recovery. When volume *dries up* at the top of a long
rally, pros start paying very close attention.

📊 CHART NEEDED: `charts/L1-03-volume-spike.png`
INSTRUMENT / TIMEFRAME: Nifty 50 or a liquid stock · 1-hour
MUST SHOW:
  - A breakout candle pushing above a clear range high
  - Volume bar under it 2–3× taller than recent bars
  - Annotation: "Volume confirms the move"

## 🇮🇳 The Indian story: the Budget-day wick

You don't need crypto for violent candles — India prints them too. On **February 1, 2021,
Budget day**, Nifty opened strong, crossed 14,000 in euphoria, then reversed over
**1,000 points intraday** to close negative — a massive upper wick on the daily chart.
Traders who chased the morning breakout bought the top of that wick; the candle itself
recorded exactly what happened: buyers pushed, sellers rejected, control changed hands
in hours. And during March 2020, Nifty's daily candles carried the same long lower
wicks as Bitcoin's May 2021 — the footprint of panic being absorbed at the lows. The
language of candles is the same on NSE, NYSE, or Binance.

## Key takeaways
- Body = who won the period; wicks = who fought and lost (Bitcoin's May 2021 lower wick
  was buyers rejecting the panic).
- Higher timeframe = signal; lower timeframe = noise. Zoom out first.
- Volume confirms or exposes a price move.

## Quick check ✅
1. A candle has a very long upper wick and a small body at the bottom. What happened?
2. Why is a 1-minute chart dangerous for beginners?
3. Price breaks above a range on tiny volume. Trust it — yes or no?

## Today's action step
Open any liquid stock on the daily chart. Find: (1) one long-upper-wick candle, (2) one
long-lower-wick candle, (3) the highest-volume day in the last month — and look up what
*news* happened on those days. You're building the reflex that connects candles to real
events, which is the whole game.

Answers: 1 — Buyers pushed up, sellers rejected them; sellers won ·
2 — Too much noise, fake moves, overtrading · 3 — No — wait for confirmation or skip

lessons.title: Points, Ticks & Lot Sizes — What a Move Is Worth

# Day 4 — Points, Ticks & Lot Sizes: What a Move Is Worth

**🎬 The day oil went below zero — and destroyed people who never read the contract**

On April 20, 2020, something happened that had never happened in market history: the
May WTI crude oil futures contract closed at **minus $37.63 per barrel**. Sellers were
paying buyers to take oil off their hands. Thousands of traders — many in India trading
US oil ETFs and contracts through apps — were wiped out. Some owed more than they put in.

Most of them had never read the contract they were trading. They didn't know what a
"barrel" unit meant for their P&L, that futures expire and force delivery mechanics,
that the contract they held was about to roll. They knew "oil is cheap, it must bounce."
They did not know **what one point of oil was worth to them**. Today you learn the
lesson those traders paid their accounts for — it's the least glamorous and most
profitable lesson in Level 1.

> 💬 **No scrolling back:** one lot of Nifty, and it moves 100 points. What's that in rupees? Take a real guess right now — type it as a reply if you're feeling brave. Most people who've traded for a year get this wrong, and the April 2020 oil traders *lost their accounts* getting it wrong. That's why today exists.

## What you'll learn
- Points vs ticks — and why the WTI crash was a contract-knowledge disaster
- Lot size / contract multiplier
- Converting a price move into rupees

## Why this lesson exists

Ask a beginner: *"Nifty moved 50 points — how much did you make?"* Most can't answer.
If you don't know what a move is worth in money **before** you trade, you're not trading —
you're the April 20, 2020 crowd, hoping.

## The vocabulary

| Term | Meaning | Example (Nifty futures) |
|---|---|---|
| **Point** | One unit of price | 24,100 → 24,150 = 50 points |
| **Tick** | Smallest price increment | Nifty = 0.05 points |
| **Lot size** | Minimum quantity per contract | Nifty futures lot = 75 (check current) |
| **Multiplier** | Lot size × 1 (for futures) | 1 point = ₹75 per lot |
| **Tick value** | Value of one tick | 0.05 × 75 = ₹3.75 |

The oil traders' fatal gap: they knew oil's price, not their exposure. WTI's contract is
1,000 barrels per contract — a $1 move = $1,000 per contract. When oil went from $18 to
-$37, that was a **-$55,000 swing per single contract**. Knowing that number beforehand
is the entire lesson.

## The only formula you need

> **Profit/Loss = Points gained × Lot size × Number of lots**

**Example:** You buy 1 lot of Nifty futures at 24,100 and exit at 24,150.
- Points gained = 50 · Lot size = 75 · **P/L = 50 × 75 × 1 = ₹3,750** (before charges)

**Same move in a stock:** buy 100 shares at ₹500, sell at ₹510 → ₹10 × 100 = **₹1,000**.

📊 CHART NEEDED: `charts/L1-04-point-move.png`
INSTRUMENT / TIMEFRAME: Nifty 50 futures · daily
MUST SHOW:
  - A clean 100–150 point swing
  - Text label: "This move = 120 points × ₹75/lot = ₹9,000 per lot"
  - Entry zone and exit zone marked with horizontal lines

## Worked examples — do these yourself

1. Bank Nifty moves 200 points. Lot size 30. You hold 2 lots. P/L?
2. A stock moves ₹12 in your favor, you hold 250 shares. P/L?
3. Nifty moves 40 points **against** you, 1 lot. P/L?

*(Answers at the bottom.)*

## 📌 Case file: the charge reality check

Every trade costs: brokerage + exchange fees + STT/CTT + GST + stamp duty. On a small
win these eat 10–20% of profits. Two implications:

1. **Tiny targets don't pay** — a 5-point scalp on Nifty is ₹375 gross; costs can take a
   third of it. (This is also why the oil ETFs' churn destroyed value even before the
   crash.)
2. **Overtrading bleeds you** — 20 round-trips a day in costs can exceed your skill edge.

Exact math returns on Day 20 — today, just know the costs exist and that *knowing your
per-point value* is what keeps them proportionate.

## 🇮🇳 The Indian story: MCX crude went negative too

The Indian trader's version of the oil disaster happened at home. On April 20–21, 2020,
MCX crude oil futures — the contract thousands of Indian commodity traders held — settled
**below zero**, the first time Indian retail saw negative prices on their screens. Traders
who'd "bought the dip" in crude because it was "cheap" learned they'd never calculated
their per-barrel exposure: a ₹-1,000/barrel settlement against their position size meant
losses exceeding their margins, with brokers making emergency margin calls through the
night. Before you trade anything in India — Nifty lot, BankNifty lot, one lot of silver
MCX — write down what ONE point costs you. That single habit separates you from both the
USO crowd and the MCX crude crowd.

## Key takeaways
- P/L = points × lot size × lots. Memorize it — the April 2020 oil crowd didn't.
- Always translate a potential move into rupees *before* entering.
- Small targets + frequent trades = death by charges.

## Quick check ✅
1. Nifty lot 75, you gain 80 points on 2 lots. P/L?
2. Why is a 5-point scalp usually a bad idea for beginners?
3. Stock at ₹1,000 → ₹1,040, you hold 50 shares. P/L?

## Today's action step
Pick 5 instruments you might trade. For each, write down: lot size, value of 1 point,
value of a 100-point move, **and what a 3× adverse gap would cost you in rupees**. That
last column — the "what if it gaps against me" number — is the one the oil traders
never wrote down. Keep this list next to your desk forever.

Answers: W1 — 200 × 30 × 2 = ₹12,000 · W2 — 12 × 250 = ₹3,000 · W3 — −40 × 75 = −₹3,000 ·
QC1 — 80 × 75 × 2 = ₹12,000 · QC2 — costs eat too large a share; noise dominates ·
QC3 — 40 × 50 = ₹2,000

lessons.title: Leverage & Margin — The Multiplier
lessons.content:
# Day 5 — Leverage & Margin: The Multiplier

**🎬 The ₹2 lakh ticket to an ₹18 lakh position**

Meet Meena. She has ₹2 lakh in her trading account, and she's bullish on the market.
Without the instrument you're about to learn, participating would be impossible: one
lot of Nifty futures represents 75 × 24,000 = **₹18 lakh of index**. Meena doesn't
have ₹18 lakh. End of story.

Except it isn't. Her broker asks for only about **₹1.5–2 lakh as margin** — a security
deposit — and lets her hold the position. That's **leverage**: the ability to control a
large position with a small deposit. It's the reason a small account can trade markets
at all, and it's available to you every single day on NSE.

Now watch the same tool do two very different jobs.

**Job one — with a plan.** Meena buys at 24,100 with a stop at 24,040 (her idea is
"wrong" below 24,040, plain and simple). Nifty rises 200 points over the next week.
Her gain: 200 × 75 = **₹15,000 — about 7.5% on her ₹2 lakh account in days.** She
controlled ₹18 lakh with ₹2 lakh, and a planned trade paid her. This is leverage doing
exactly what it was built for.

**Job two — without a plan.** Ravi, same account, same lot — but no stop, because
"it'll come back." Nifty falls 500 points in a bad week. His loss: 500 × 75 =
**₹37,500 — nearly 19% of his account**, gone. Not because leverage is evil. Because
Ravi's plan was a feeling.

Same tool. Same market. The multiplier amplified whatever was attached to it — Meena's
plan, or Ravi's hope. **Leverage is not good or bad. It simply multiplies your process.**
Today you learn to make sure what's attached to it is a plan.

> 💬 **One word will do:** Meena made ₹15,000 in a week on a planned trade. Ravi lost ₹37,500 on hope. Same tool, same market, same month. What do you think the real difference between them was? Prediction? Luck? Personality? Note your one word — then see if it survives today's lesson.

## What you'll learn
- What leverage and margin actually are (Meena's version)
- How the multiplier works in both directions
- The leverage you're actually using — and the two rules that make it safe

## What is leverage?

> **Leverage lets you control a large position with a small security deposit called
> margin.** You own the profit or loss of the full position — the margin is just the
> deposit.

Meena's example above is 9× leverage (₹18 lakh position ÷ ₹2 lakh margin). Her broker
holds the margin as security and settles her P&L in cash daily (that's "mark-to-market"
— profits added, losses deducted, every day).

## How the multiplier works

| Nifty moves | Against 1 lot (75) | On ₹2 lakh margin | With Meena's stop? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 points | ₹3,750 | 1.9% | Never reached |
| 200 points (favor) | +₹15,000 | +7.5% | Banked |
| 500 points (against) | ₹37,500 | 18.8% | Exited at −₹4,500 |

See the design: with a stop, the multiplier works **for** her on good trades and the
stop caps it on bad ones. Without a stop, there's no cap at all. The tool didn't change
— the plan did.

## The margin call

If losses eat into your margin, the broker asks for more money — a **margin call**.
Can't add funds? The position is closed for you, at whatever the market gives, usually
the worst moment. A stop loss you chose beats a margin call the broker chose, every
time. (Days 18–20 will make your stop and your size automatic.)

## The leverage you're actually using

Most beginners think: *"I don't use leverage, I trade stocks."* Check again:

| Instrument | Typical leverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Equity delivery (CNC) | 1× | No leverage |
| Equity intraday (MIS) | 3–5× | Broker blocks a fraction of value |
| Futures | 5–10× | Daily mark-to-market |
| Options buying | Premium at risk | Can go to zero; max loss = premium paid |
| Options selling | 5–8× | Bigger obligations — we'll cover this much later |

Notice: options *buying* is the only one where the most you can lose is fixed upfront —
the premium you paid. That's one reason beginners start there.

## The two rules that make leverage safe

1. **Every leveraged position carries a stop loss chosen by you, from the first second.**
   (Day 18: placed beyond the structure, not by feeling.)
2. **Position size comes from the formula, never from the margin available.** The broker
   will happily let you use all your margin. The formula often says use a quarter of it.
   (Day 20.)

With those two rules, leverage is what lets a ₹2 lakh account build like a much larger
one. Without them, the multiplier runs the other way. Same as Meena and Ravi — the tool
was identical.

## 🇮🇳 The Indian story: crores of traders, almost none with these two rules

India runs one of the world's biggest leveraged retail markets, and SEBI measured the
result: in its FY22–FY24 study, **93% of individual F&O traders lost money**, average
losses around **₹2 lakh per trader**, total retail F&O losses near **₹1.8 lakh crore**.
Read that data carefully, though — it doesn't say leverage lost the money. It says
traders without a written stop and a calculated size lost the money. The winners in
SEBI's data used the same leverage, the same products, the same market. The difference
was never the tool. Over the next fifteen days, you install the two rules above — and
the same products that drained ₹1.8 lakh crore become usable, on your terms.

## Key takeaways
- Leverage = controlling a large position with a small margin deposit. It's the tool that
  lets small accounts trade big markets at all. (Meena: ₹18 lakh position, ₹2 lakh
  deposit, +7.5% in a planned week.)
- The multiplier runs both directions — the stop and the size decide which direction
  matters to you. Never the broker's margin limit.
- Two rules make leverage safe: your stop on every position, size from the formula.

## Quick check ✅
1. One Nifty lot = ₹18 lakh position on ₹2 lakh margin. Nifty rises 200 points. Gain in
   ₹, and roughly what % of the margin?
2. What's the difference between a stop loss and a margin call — who chooses each one?
3. Which instrument in the table has its maximum loss fixed upfront?

## Today's action step
Open your broker's margin calculator. Type in one Nifty futures trade and one intraday
stock trade. Write down the margin each blocks, and your implied leverage (position
value ÷ margin). Then compute: if your stop were hit on each, what % of your account
would you lose? That last number — not the leverage number — is the only one that
matters. You're about to learn to control it precisely.

Answers: 1 — 200 × 75 = ₹15,000 ≈ +7.5% of ₹2 lakh ·
2 — Stop loss: you choose the exit level before entering. Margin call: the broker forces
an exit when your deposit runs out · 3 — Options buying (max loss = the premium you paid)

lessons.title: Long vs Short, Spreads & Slippage
lessons.content:
# Day 6 — Long vs Short, Spreads & Slippage

**🎬 The 15 minutes that broke currency brokers**

On January 15, 2015, at 9:30 AM Swiss time, the Swiss National Bank — without warning — cancelled its three-year-old promise to keep the Swiss franc from rising too fast against the euro. In roughly **15
minutes**, the franc surged 30–40%. Within days, **Alpari UK was bankrupt** and
FXCM — the largest US retail forex broker — needed a **$225 million emergency loan** to
survive. What killed them wasn't the direction — it was the **plumbing**: during those
minutes, bid-ask spreads on EUR/CHF blew from fractions of a pip to several *dollars*
wide, and stop losses filled miles from their triggers. Slippage did the rest.

The SNB shock is the perfect story for today, because it contains all three of our
subjects: making money in both directions (franc *buyers* made fortunes that day),
the spread, and slippage — the two hidden costs that quietly tax every trade you place.

> 💬 **Have you ever…** bought a stock, watched it go UP, and *still* lost money on the trade? If yes, today's lesson will feel like someone reading your diary. If no — it's coming for you eventually, and the Swiss franc story is why. What's your guess: what invisible thing ate that profit?

## What you'll learn
- Going long vs going short
- The bid-ask spread (and how it blew out on January 15, 2015)
- Slippage — and when it hurts most

## Long vs short

**Going long** = buying first, selling later. Profit when price rises.
*(Buy at 100, sell at 110 → +10.)*

**Going short** = selling first, buying back later. Profit when price falls.
*(Sell at 100, buy back at 90 → +10.)*

Shorting feels strange to beginners ("how can I sell what I don't own?"), but in futures
and intraday equity your broker facilitates it — you settle the difference in cash.
And the franc story shows why it matters: while EUR/CHF longs were being destroyed,
traders short EUR/CHF — or long CHF — made some of the fastest money in currency history.
> **Key insight:** long and short are symmetric. Professionals are as comfortable
> shorting as buying.

## The bid-ask spread

At any moment there are two prices:

- **Bid** — the highest price a buyer is currently offering
- **Ask** — the lowest price a seller is currently accepting

The gap = the **spread**, and you always pay it: buyers lift the ask, sellers hit the bid.

| | Bid | Ask | Spread |
|---|---|---|---|
| Liquid stock (e.g., Reliance) | 500.00 | 500.05 | ₹0.05 (tiny) |
| Illiquid stock | 100.00 | 101.20 | ₹1.20 (1.2%!) |
| EUR/CHF, Jan 15 2015, ~9:31 AM | "who knows" | "who knows" | effectively unmeasurable |

On liquid instruments the toll is negligible. On illiquid ones — and in panics — the
spread alone can exceed your entire expected profit.

## Slippage

**Slippage** = the difference between the price you *expected* and the price you *got*:

- **Market orders** in fast markets (you take whatever's left in the queue)
- **Gaps** — price jumps over your level between click and fill
- **News shocks** — liquidity vanishes for seconds (the SNB morning)

> Slippage is usually tiny — until the one day it isn't. Stops don't guarantee prices;
> they guarantee *an exit*, at whatever the market gives. On January 15, 2015, many
> stop losses on CHF pairs filled 10–20% away from their triggers. The stops worked
> exactly as designed. The design has limits.

## The practical rules

1. Trade liquid instruments only — check average daily volume first.
2. Limit orders for entries (you choose your price).
3. Size positions so a slippy stop *hurts, never kills*.
4. No new trades into major news events — the SNB taught the world that lesson free of charge.

📊 CHART NEEDED: `charts/L1-06-spread-slippage.png`
INSTRUMENT / TIMEFRAME: Two 1-minute panels — one very liquid stock, one illiquid stock
MUST SHOW:
  - Bid/ask levels marked on both
  - Liquid panel: tight spread, "≈ 0.01%"
  - Illiquid panel: wide spread, "≈ 1.2% — profit gone before you start"

## 🇮🇳 The Indian story: Yes Bank's circuit-locked exits

India's own slippage machine is the **price circuit**. When Yes Bank collapsed in March
2020, the stock hit its lower circuit day after day — meaning the price was *locked* at
the day's limit with a queue of sellers and almost no buyers. Stop losses were useless:
you couldn't exit at any price, because the exchange wouldn't let the price fall further
that session. Sellers watched helplessly as the stock ground from ₹30 to ₹20 to ₹12 over
circuit-locked sessions. That's slippage in its purest Indian form — the market not
filling you at your price, but refusing to fill you at *any* price. Liquidity isn't a
theory here; on NSE, some days it simply switches off.

## Key takeaways
- Short = selling first; symmetric to long (the franc surge rewarded shorts brutally).
- Spread is a toll on every trade; slippage is a tax on fast markets — both were weapons
  on Jan 15, 2015.
- Liquidity is protection. Thin markets are where beginners donate money.

## Quick check ✅
1. Stock bid 250.00 / ask 250.10. You market-buy 100 shares, then market-sell instantly. P/L before charges?
2. Why do stop losses sometimes fill far below the trigger?
3. Long or short: you profit if price *falls*?

## Today's action step
Watch the order book (market depth) of a liquid stock for 5 minutes — see the spread
breathe. Then open an illiquid stock's depth. That visual difference is the SNB story
at 0.01% scale. You'll never trade illiquid again.

Answers: 1 — buy 250.10, sell 250.00 → −₹10 (the spread) ·
2 — Stop becomes a market order; price gaps/slips before your exit fills · 3 — Short

lessons.title: The Three Types of Analysis
lessons.content:
# Day 7 — The Three Types of Analysis

**🎬 Three men, one housing market, three completely different trades**

In 2005–2007, while Wall Street was printing money on US housing, three very different
analysts looked at the same market:

**The fundamental analyst** — Michael Burry's team at Scion Capital — read thousands of
mortgage documents, ran the default math, and concluded the loans inside mortgage bonds
were garbage. They bought insurance against those home-loan bonds failing, and held it for about a year and a half while looking *wrong* — the trade bled money until it didn't.
When 2008 came, Scion made roughly **$700 million** for its investors. His lens:
*"what is this actually worth?"*

**The technical analyst** didn't need to read a single loan file. By 2007, charts of
homebuilder stocks, mortgage insurers, and bank indices had broken their multi-year
uptrends — lower highs, neckline breaks — months before the headlines. The price action
*told* you credit was cracking. His lens: *"what is price doing right now?"*

**The sentiment analyst** watched the crowd: in 2006–07, CNBC ran "flip this house"
segments, taxi drivers discussed condo pre-sales, and mortgage originators handed loans
to anyone with a pulse. When *everyone* is bullish and the last skeptic has bought —
that's not confirmation, that's exhaustion. His lens: *"what is everyone feeling?"*

One market, three lenses, three valid edges. Today you learn all three — and which one
this course is built on.

> 💬 **Pick one, honestly:** three lenses — worth (A), behavior (B), mood (C). Which one have YOU actually been using till now, even accidentally? Most people are quietly shocked when they realize. Note A, B, or C — no judgment, we all start somewhere.

## What you'll learn
- Technical, fundamental, and sentiment analysis
- What question each one answers
- Which style fits which trader

## 1. Fundamental analysis — *"What is it worth?"*

Revenue, profits, debt, management, industry trends, macro. Home country: investors and
position traders. Strength: catches big moves early, ignores noise. Weakness: *"the market
can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent"* — Burry's investors nearly pulled
out before the payoff, because being early looks exactly like being wrong.

## 2. Technical analysis — *"What is it doing right now?"*

Trends, levels, patterns, volume — no opinions, only behavior. Works on anything liquid
(Nifty, gold, Bitcoin, USDINR — same rules); gives exact entries, stops, targets.
Weakness: reads the *present*, not the future.

## 3. Sentiment analysis — *"What is everyone feeling?"*

Put-call ratios, open interest shifts, funding rates, news euphoria. Extremes in
sentiment often mark tops (2007 housing) and bottoms (March 2020, when panic peaked and
so did the selling). Weakness: hard to time; the crowd can stay greedy for a long time.

📊 CHART NEEDED: `charts/L1-07-three-analyses.png`
INSTRUMENT / TIMEFRAME: One stock · daily · last 6 months
MUST SHOW (three annotation styles on the SAME chart):
  - Fundamental: an earnings date + arrow "earnings gap — business repriced"
  - Technical: trendline + support zone + breakout arrow
  - Sentiment: at a local top, "news euphoria, everyone's bullish → reversal"

## Which one do you use?

> **Fundamentals decide *what* to watch. Sentiment warns *when* the crowd is extreme.
> Technicals decide *when and where* to pull the trigger.**

## Why this course teaches technicals first

Exact, testable rules (enter here, stop here, target here); works across every liquid
market; fundamentals can be added later as a filter, sentiment as a warning light.

## 🇮🇳 The Indian story: Paytm's listing and Reliance's raise — the same year, opposite lenses

2021 gave you both lenses in one year. **Fundamental:** in April–June 2020, while the
market was crashing, Reliance Industries raised **₹1.52 lakh crore in 58 days** selling
stakes in Jio — investors read the *business* and paid up even mid-panic. The stock led
Nifty's recovery. **Sentiment:** in November 2021, Paytm's IPO listed at ₹1,955 against
a ₹2,150 issue price and closed **−27% on day one**, then fell toward ₹500 as IPO euphoria
— India's own dot-com moment — deflated. Everyone wanted in; the crowd's excitement WAS
the warning. Same market, same year: one trade from the fundamentals, one lesson from
the mood.

## Key takeaways
- Fundamental = worth · Technical = behavior · Sentiment = mood. (2008 showed all three
  working in parallel.)
- Professionals blend all three; beginners master technicals first.
- Every tool answers a different question — confusion comes from asking the wrong tool.

## Quick check ✅
1. Which analysis type gives you an exact stop-loss level?
2. "The stock is undervalued, I should buy" — which lens? What's its risk?
3. At an extreme bullish sentiment, a contrarian starts thinking about…?

## Today's action step
Open the chart of one stock you like. Ask the three questions out loud — What is it
worth? What is it doing? What is everyone feeling? Notice how each question pulls you
toward a different decision. That awareness is the lesson.

Answers: 1 — Technical · 2 — Fundamental; can stay "undervalued" (falling) far longer
than expected · 3 — Selling/shorting, or at least taking profits

lessons.title: Find Your Trading Style + Level 1 Quiz
lessons.content:
# Day 8 — Find Your Trading Style (Level 1 Finale)

**🎬 The Turtle experiment — proof that style is a system, not a personality**

In 1983, two legendary commodities traders made a bet. Richard Dennis believed great
traders were **made** — teachable. His partner Bill Eckhardt believed they were **born**.
To settle it, Dennis recruited about 20 people with *no trading experience* — a
security guard, a blackjack player, an accountant — gave them a simple mechanical
trend-following system and strict risk rules, and let them trade real money.

The "Turtles" went on to earn a reported **$175 million+** in aggregate. Here's what
matters for today's lesson: the Turtle system was a **swing/position system**. It held
trades for days to weeks, risked a fixed small fraction per trade, and ignored all
intraday noise. Dennis deliberately picked the style * beginners could execute without
losing their minds* — not the fastest, not the flashiest, the *survivable* one.

Forty years later, the lesson is unchanged: the best style for you isn't the one that
makes the most money in theory — it's the one your life and your nervous system can
execute without breaking. Today you pick yours. Then you take the Level 1 quiz. 🎓

> 💬 **Gut-check, no thinking:** you enter a trade, and ten minutes later your phone shows it's down 3%. What's your honest first move — (a) refresh every two minutes, (b) close the app and check after lunch, or (c) buy more at the "discount"? Note a, b, or c. Your answer matters more than any quiz in this level.

## What you'll learn
- The four trading styles
- How to choose yours based on time and personality
- Level 1 final quiz (10 questions)

## The four styles

| Style | Holding period | Time needed | Stress level |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Scalping** | Seconds–minutes | Full day, fast reflexes | 🔴 Extreme |
| **Day trading** | Minutes–hours | Market hours, focused | 🟠 High |
| **Swing trading** | Days–weeks | 30–60 min/day, after close | 🟡 Medium |
| **Position trading** | Weeks–months | A few hours per week | 🟢 Low |

📊 CHART NEEDED: `charts/L1-08-styles.png`
INSTRUMENT / TIMEFRAME: Nifty 50 · daily chart with a 5-minute inset
MUST SHOW:
  - On the daily: 2–3 swings labeled "Swing trade — held days"
  - On the inset: one intraday move labeled "Day trade — held minutes"
  - A tiny zone labeled "Scalp — seconds"

## Choose based on your life, not your ego

Ask honestly:

1. **Time:** Can you watch markets 9:15–3:30 daily? → day trading is possible. Job + family?
   → swing trading. That's most people, and the Turtles proved it's enough.
2. **Temperament:** Do fast decisions excite you or wreck you? Do losses at 9:45 AM ruin
   your whole day? Swing trading forgives a busy schedule *and* a sensitive nervous system.
3. **Capital:** Smaller accounts can't absorb scalping's costs and slippage. Swing
   trading stretches capital further.

> **Course recommendation:** start with **swing trading** — the Turtle way. Higher
> timeframes = less noise, fewer decisions, more time to think. You can always go
> faster later. Going from fast to slow is much harder than slow to fast.

## ⚠️ One thing before you go

Whatever style you pick, the next three levels apply to all of them. Support/resistance,
risk management, psychology — universal. Style is just your seat on the same plane.

---

# 🎓 LEVEL 1 FINAL QUIZ

Note your answers (e.g., `1b 2a 3c...`). Score 8+ to unlock Level 2.

**1.** The price on your screen updates when…
a) the exchange recalculates averages  b) a buyer and seller agree on a trade  c) every second, automatically

**2.** You want to buy only if price drops to your level. Order type?
a) Market  b) Stop-market  c) Limit

**3.** A long upper wick on a candle means…
a) strong buying  b) buyers pushed up and got rejected  c) low volume

**4.** Nifty lot = 75, you gain 60 points on 3 lots. P/L?
a) ₹4,500  b) ₹13,500  c) ₹450

**5.** What causes a margin call?
a) Broker fees  b) Losses eating your margin below requirement  c) Trading after hours

**6.** A stop loss guarantees…
a) your exact exit price  b) an exit — at whatever price the market gives  c) profit protection

**7.** The bid-ask spread is…
a) a broker fee  b) the gap between highest buyer and lowest seller  c) the daily price range

**8.** Selling first and buying back lower is called…
a) Hedging  b) Shorting  c) Arbitrage

**9.** Which question does technical analysis answer?
a) What is it worth?  b) What is the crowd feeling?  c) What is price doing right now?

**10.** For someone with a full-time job, the recommended starting style is…
a) Scalping  b) Swing trading  c) Position trading only

<details><summary>Answer key (don't peek before submitting)</summary>
1b · 2c · 3b · 4b (60×75×3) · 5b · 6b · 7b · 8b · 9c · 10b</details>

---

## 🎓 Graduation message (Day 8 evening, your end-of-day reflection)

> "You just finished Level 1: Foundations. You now understand markets the way the
> Flash Crash, the franc shock, and the Turtles teach them — from the mechanics up.
> Level 2 unlocks tomorrow: the Technical Toolkit. 🎓"

## 🇮🇳 The Indian story: the Big Bull held Titan for decades

Rakesh Jhunjhunwala — the "Big Bull" of Dalal Street — bought Titan in the early 2000s
for a few rupees per share and held it for **two decades** as it compounded past ₹2,000+
(adjusted). That is position trading at its extreme: weeks-to-months becomes
years-to-decades when the trend and the business keep paying. On the other end of the
Indian spectrum, the intraday F&O crowd trades seconds-to-hours — and SEBI's data says
93% of them lose. India doesn't lack a style debate; it lacks survival statistics. The
Turtles chose the survivable style. Jhunjhunwala proved what it compounds into. Same
lesson, two continents.

## Key takeaways
- Style must fit your real life — time, temperament, capital. The Turtles won with the
  *survivable* style, not the fastest one.
- Start slow (swing), speed up later if you want to.
- Quiz ≥ 8/10 → Level 2 tomorrow.
